modules.title: Welcome to Scientific Programming
modules.description: Understand how a scientist turns a research question into reproducible instructions, then create the first checkpoint of your Vegetation Data Explorer notebook.
modules.lessonContent:
## Learning Outcome

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain scientific programming as the translation of a scientific question into precise, repeatable instructions. You will also be able to create, name, run, save and explain a Jupyter notebook containing your first Python instruction.

**Prerequisites:** None. You do not need to know Python, terminals, files or notebooks. Allow about 60–90 minutes and work slowly enough to describe what each action does.

**Module project:** You will create `Vegetation_Data_Explorer.ipynb`. This is not a disposable exercise. You will extend the same notebook throughout all twelve lessons.

## Why This Matters

Remote sensing research is built from chains of decisions: which observations to use, how to screen them, which transformation to apply, how to summarize uncertainty and how to present the result. If those decisions exist only as mouse clicks or remembered steps, another scientist cannot reliably repeat them—and neither can you six months later.

Programming makes a method explicit. A well-written instruction can be inspected, rerun on another field plot and corrected without reconstructing the whole analysis. This is why remote sensing teams use code for tasks such as reading field measurements, masking clouds, aligning rasters, calculating vegetation indices and generating maps.

Code does **not** replace scientific judgement. Python can calculate exactly what you request even when the request is ecologically inappropriate. Your job as a Remote Sensing Scientist is to connect a defensible question, suitable data, transparent computation and cautious interpretation.

## Scientific Context

You have joined a research group studying Baltic coastal meadows. The group has published a table of plant community traits collected at four coastal wetland sites. The table contains 120 quadrat observations and 25 fields, including `SampleID`, `site`, `plantcommunity`, `Sp_richness` and community-weighted trait measurements.

You will not open the full table yet. A beginner should first understand the instrument used to inspect it. In Lessons 1–3, you will build that foundation with very small examples. Lesson 7 will introduce the published table; later lessons will work directly with it.

Your continuing scientific question is:

> How can field measurements help us describe and compare vegetation patterns across Baltic coastal meadow plots?

Today you create the research record in which that question will develop.

## Concept

### Programming is an explicit method

A **program** is a sequence of instructions written in a form a computer can execute. The computer does not infer your intention. It follows the instructions and syntax you provide.

**Scientific programming** uses those instructions to produce, check or communicate scientific evidence. It includes more than calculation. A scientific workflow records where data came from, which assumptions were made, what was changed, what output was produced and how that output was interpreted.

Think of the relationship this way:

- the **scientist** defines the question and decides what counts as credible evidence;
- the **program** records the computational method;
- the **computer** executes that method exactly;
- the **scientist** checks the output and decides what it means.

### Why scientists use Python

Python is an open-source programming language with a large scientific ecosystem. The same language can work with field tables, satellite rasters, vector boundaries, time series, statistical models and machine-learning workflows. Its syntax is relatively readable, which helps a research team review the method rather than hide it behind a proprietary sequence of clicks.

Python is not scientifically correct by default. A program can use the wrong unit, confuse a missing value with zero or calculate a precise answer to a weak question. The value of Python is that the steps are visible and repeatable enough to inspect.

### Why a notebook rather than a Word document?

A Word document is useful for a final narrative. A Jupyter notebook is designed for an evolving computational investigation. One notebook can contain:

- **Markdown cells** for questions, methods, explanations and interpretation;
- **code cells** for executable Python instructions;
- **outputs** such as text, tables, figures, maps and error messages.

Keeping these together connects a claim with the instruction that produced its evidence. A notebook is not automatically reproducible, however. Cells can be run out of order, files can be missing and assumptions can remain undocumented. A professional notebook is saved, rerun from a clean state and written so another scientist can follow it.

### How a computer executes a notebook cell

When you run a code cell, Jupyter sends the text in that cell to a running Python **kernel**. The kernel is the process that reads the instruction, checks whether the syntax is valid, performs the requested operation and returns output or an error. Within a cell, Python normally works from top to bottom.

An error is not evidence that you are “bad at programming.” It is a diagnostic message: Python reached an instruction it could not interpret or complete. Scientific programmers learn to read that message, locate the relevant line and change one thing at a time.

### Create the portfolio notebook

A **file** is a saved digital item with a name. A **folder** groups files. The ending `.ipynb` tells your computer that this file is a Jupyter notebook.

Use the Jupyter environment provided by your institution if you have one. If you do not, open the free browser-based [Try Jupyter environment](https://jupyter.org/try-jupyter/lab/). It requires no terminal or installation. Browser workspaces can be cleared, so download a copy at the end of every lesson.

1. Open JupyterLab and create a new **Python 3** notebook.
2. Find the notebook name, usually `Untitled.ipynb`, near the top.
3. Rename it exactly `Vegetation_Data_Explorer.ipynb`. Use underscores rather than spaces so the name remains easy to use across operating systems.
4. Notice the empty rectangle on the page. This is a **cell**. Confirm that its type is **Code**.
5. Save the notebook. Saving updates the file; downloading creates a separate copy on your computer.

## Visual Explanation

![Diagram showing a scientific question moving through a notebook plan, code cell, Python execution, output and scientific interpretation.](lesson-media/images/scientific-programming-execution.svg)

The arrows across the top show execution. The lower loop is equally important: only the scientist can judge whether an output answers the ecological question, whether the assumptions are reasonable and what should be revised.

## Worked Example

Click the first code cell. Type the following, but **do not run it yet**:

```python
print()
```

Add a second code cell and type:

```python
print("Vegetation Data Explorer")
print("Study system: Baltic coastal meadows")
print("Question: How does vegetation vary among field plots?")
```

The worked example contains four instructions in total. Each instruction is short, but each has an observable effect.

## Predict Before Running

Before touching the Run button, write a prediction in your private lesson notes:

1. Will `print()` display the word “print”, an empty-looking line or an error?
2. In what order will the three messages from the second cell appear?
3. Will Python understand the ecological meaning of the question, or only display its characters?

Now run the first cell with **Shift + Enter**. Then run the second cell the same way.

The first output area looks empty because `print()` produced only a new line. The second output should be:

```text
Vegetation Data Explorer
Study system: Baltic coastal meadows
Question: How does vegetation vary among field plots?
```

If your output differs, compare one character at a time before replacing the whole cell.

## Code Walkthrough

1. `print()` names Python’s built-in `print` function. The parentheses mean “call this function now.” Because there is nothing inside the parentheses, the function writes only a line break. The kernel still executed a valid instruction.
2. `print("Vegetation Data Explorer")` calls the same function with one piece of text. The quotation marks tell Python where the text begins and ends. Python displays the characters without the quotation marks.
3. `print("Study system: Baltic coastal meadows")` is the next instruction, so its message appears on the next output line.
4. `print("Question: How does vegetation vary among field plots?")` displays your working question. Python does not evaluate whether the question is scientifically useful; it only follows the display instruction.

This distinction is fundamental: **execution answers “Did the computer follow the instruction?” Scientific interpretation answers “Does the result support the investigation?”**

## Common Mistakes

### Typing Python into a Markdown cell

**Why beginners make it:** Code cells and Markdown cells occupy similar-looking rectangles.

**How to recognize it:** The notebook displays `print("...")` as formatted text instead of producing output.

**How to fix it:** Select the cell, change its type to **Code**, then run it again.

### Using curved quotation marks

**Why beginners make it:** Word processors and phones often replace straight quotes with typographic quotes.

**How to recognize it:** Python reports a `SyntaxError` and points near the quotation mark.

**How to fix it:** Retype both quotation marks directly in the notebook as straight `"` characters.

### Leaving out a quotation mark or parenthesis

**Why beginners make it:** The punctuation is visually small and unfamiliar.

**How to recognize it:** The cell does not complete and Python reports invalid syntax or an unclosed string/parenthesis.

**How to fix it:** Check pairs from the outside inward: one opening parenthesis, two quotation marks and one closing parenthesis.

### Running cells out of order

**Why beginners make it:** Jupyter lets you run any cell at any time.

**How to recognize it:** Execution numbers are out of sequence, or a result changes after cells are rerun in a different order.

**How to fix it:** Before submitting, restart the kernel and use **Run All**. A clean top-to-bottom run is a basic reproducibility check.

## Guided Practice

Build the opening of your notebook step by step.

1. Insert a Markdown cell at the top and enter:

   ```markdown
   # Vegetation Data Explorer
   **Study system:** Baltic coastal meadows
   **Working question:** How does vegetation vary among field plots?
   ```

2. Run the Markdown cell. It should render as a title and two labelled statements.
3. Keep the two code cells from the worked example below it.
4. Add another Markdown cell titled `## First execution note`.
5. In that cell, write two sentences: what `print()` instructed the computer to do, and why its blank-looking output is still a result.
6. Save the notebook. Then download a copy into a folder you can find again, such as a new folder named `Vegetation_Data_Explorer`.
7. Close the browser tab, reopen the downloaded notebook in your chosen environment and confirm the content is present. This checks that you understand the difference between a temporary browser session and a saved file.

## Independent Challenge

Without copying the worked example, add one code cell that prints:

- your name or researcher identifier;
- one ecological feature you want to understand in coastal meadows;
- one type of remote sensing evidence that might eventually help, such as UAV imagery or a vegetation index.

Before running it, predict the order of the three output lines. Then add a Markdown cell explaining which parts are instructions, which parts are output and which part is your scientific judgement.

Keep this challenge small. The purpose is not to learn more Python syntax; it is to make the execution model clear.

## Scientific Interpretation

Your output does not yet describe vegetation. It confirms that a transparent computational record can execute and preserve an instruction. That is a legitimate first checkpoint, but it is not ecological evidence.

A scientist should be able to distinguish among:

- **method record:** the Markdown and code you wrote;
- **execution evidence:** the output showing that Python ran the code;
- **scientific evidence:** measurements or derived results relevant to the research question;
- **interpretation:** your reasoned explanation of what those results mean and what they do not establish.

This distinction will prevent attractive maps or precise numbers from being mistaken for valid conclusions later in the Academy.

## Reflection

Write short answers in your private lesson notes:

1. Which decisions in the notebook belong to the scientist, and which actions belong to the computer?
2. What can a notebook preserve that a final Word report usually cannot preserve as directly?
3. How could running notebook cells out of order weaken reproducibility?
4. What would you need, beyond printed text, before making a claim about Baltic coastal meadow vegetation?

## Submission

Submit all three parts through the lesson task panel:

- **Notebook:** `Vegetation_Data_Explorer.ipynb` with the title, scientific question, worked example, first execution note and independent challenge.
- **Screenshot:** one image showing the notebook title, at least one code cell and its visible output.
- **Written answer:** 120–180 words explaining what scientific programming is and why a computer can execute code without understanding coastal ecology.

Before upload, restart the kernel and run all cells from top to bottom. The notebook is ready when it opens cleanly, the cells run without an unintended error and the written interpretation distinguishes output from evidence.

## Portfolio Artifact

**Artifact 01 — Environment notebook**

This first checkpoint demonstrates that you can create a named scientific notebook, combine narrative with executable instructions, preserve output and explain the division of responsibility between scientist and computer. Do not create a replacement notebook for Lesson 2; extend this one.

## Further Reading

- [Baltic coastal plant traits 2024 dataset record and citation](https://zenodo.org/records/20083250)
- [Project Jupyter: Try Jupyter in your browser](https://jupyter.org/try)
- [Project Jupyter documentation: getting started](https://docs.jupyter.org/en/latest/start/index.html)

modules.title: Variables and Scientific Data
modules.description: Represent one real vegetation plot with clear names and scientifically appropriate text, numeric, Boolean and missing values—without losing their meaning.
modules.lessonContent:
## Learning Outcome

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to represent one ecological field observation in Python by binding meaningful variable names to strings, integers, floating-point numbers, Boolean values and `None`. You will be able to justify each choice from its scientific meaning rather than from appearance alone.

**Prerequisites:** Complete Lesson 1 and open the same `Vegetation_Data_Explorer.ipynb` notebook. You should be able to create a code cell, predict what it will do, run it and save the notebook.

## Why This Matters

Remote sensing workflows combine different kinds of information. A plot identifier is text even when it contains digits. Species richness is a count. A measured value may contain decimals. A quality-control flag can record yes or no. A measurement that was not collected must remain distinct from a measured zero.

If these meanings are represented carelessly, later calculations can become invalid without producing an obvious error. For example, treating a missing biomass measurement as zero would falsely describe “no biomass” rather than “not measured.” Treating an identifier as a number could remove meaningful leading zeros. Data type choices are therefore part of scientific data management, not merely Python syntax.

## Scientific Context

The first row of the published Baltic coastal plant traits table describes quadrat `SALS1` at the Saardu site. Among its recorded values are:

- `SampleID`: `SALS1`;
- `site`: `Saardu`;
- `plantcommunity`: `LS`;
- `Sp_richness`: `7`;
- `Elevation`: `0.53`;
- an above-ground biomass value is present.

The Zenodo record does not currently include a field-level data dictionary with units. We can use the published field names and raw values, but we must not silently invent units or expand codes such as `LS` without documentation. In this lesson, the name `elevation_value` deliberately avoids claiming a unit. Verifying definitions and units will be part of the real-data workflow later.

You are now extending your notebook from a project introduction into a structured description of one field plot.

## Concept

A **variable** is a meaningful name that Python binds to a value. Read the instruction

`site_name = "Saardu"`

as “bind the name `site_name` to the text value `"Saardu"`.” The equals sign performs an **assignment**. It does not mean that the two sides are interchangeable in the mathematical sense.

A good variable name acts like a careful label on a field sample. Python names cannot contain spaces, so scientific programmers often use `snake_case`: lowercase words joined by underscores. Names such as `species_richness` or `biomass_sampled` preserve more meaning than `x` or `value1`.

For one plot, we need five kinds of values:

### String: text or an identifier

A **string** is text enclosed in quotation marks. `"SALS1"` and `"Saardu"` are strings. The digit in `"SALS1"` does not make it numeric; the whole value identifies a sample and is not used for arithmetic.

### Integer: a whole-number count

An **integer** is a whole number such as `7`. Species richness is recorded as the number of species in the quadrat, so a whole-number count is appropriate.

### Float: a number with a decimal component

A **float** represents a numeric value such as `0.530`. The name comes from “floating point.” A float can participate in calculations, but the number alone is incomplete scientific metadata. Its field definition, method and unit must still be known.

### Boolean: one of two logical states

A **Boolean** is either `True` or `False`, with capital first letters in Python. `biomass_sampled = True` records that a biomass value is present for this plot. It does not describe how much biomass was measured.

### None: no value is present

`None` is Python’s special marker for the absence of a value. It is not the text `"None"`, not an empty statement and not zero. In this notebook, `field_note = None` means that you have not added a separate field note. Later, data-analysis libraries may display missing tabular values differently, but the scientific principle remains: absence is not zero.

## Visual Explanation

![Diagram showing meaningful Python variable names connected to text, count, decimal, Boolean and no-value examples from the SALS1 plot.](lesson-media/images/scientific-variable-bindings.svg)

The arrow matters. A name refers to a value. The name should communicate scientific meaning, while metadata communicates the definition, method and unit that code alone cannot supply.

## Worked Example

Add a Markdown heading `## Lesson 2 — One vegetation plot` to your notebook. Under it, create a code cell and type the following. Do not run it yet.

```python
plot_id = "SALS1"
site_name = "Saardu"
species_richness = 7
elevation_value = 0.530
biomass_sampled = True
field_note = None

print(plot_id)
print(site_name)
print(species_richness)
print(elevation_value)
print(biomass_sampled)
print(field_note)
```

This example contains thirteen lines, including one blank line used for readability.

## Predict Before Running

Before running the cell, write your predictions in a Markdown cell or private lesson notes:

1. Which output values will appear with quotation marks?
2. Will Python display `0.530` exactly as typed, or can its display omit a trailing zero?
3. What will appear for `field_note`?
4. Does `True` tell you the amount of biomass?

Now run the cell. The expected output is:

```text
SALS1
Saardu
7
0.53
True
None
```

Python does not display the quotation marks because they mark string syntax rather than stored characters. It displays `0.530` as `0.53` because both notations represent the same numeric value; formatting precision is separate from the stored value.

## Code Walkthrough

1. `plot_id = "SALS1"` binds a descriptive name to a string identifier. The value stays text because it labels a sample.
2. `site_name = "Saardu"` stores the published site name as a string.
3. `species_richness = 7` stores a whole-number count as an integer.
4. `elevation_value = 0.530` stores the published decimal as a float. The variable name does not assert an undocumented unit.
5. `biomass_sampled = True` stores a Boolean statement: this row contains a biomass observation.
6. `field_note = None` records that your notebook has no additional field note for this plot.
7. The blank line performs no operation. It separates data definition from display instructions for a human reader.
8. `print(plot_id)` asks Python to retrieve the value currently bound to `plot_id` and display it.
9. `print(site_name)` retrieves and displays the site string.
10. `print(species_richness)` displays the integer count.
11. `print(elevation_value)` displays the float in Python’s compact default format.
12. `print(biomass_sampled)` displays the Boolean value `True`.
13. `print(field_note)` displays `None`, making the absence visible rather than silently converting it to zero or text.

## Common Mistakes

### Writing unquoted text

**Why beginners make it:** Saardu looks like an ordinary label rather than code.

**How to recognize it:** `site_name = Saardu` produces a `NameError` because Python looks for a variable named `Saardu`.

**How to fix it:** Put literal text inside straight quotation marks: `site_name = "Saardu"`.

### Adding quotes around every value

**Why beginners make it:** Quotation marks can feel like a general way to “protect” data.

**How to recognize it:** A count such as `"7"` is text, so later arithmetic will not behave like count arithmetic.

**How to fix it:** Ask what the value means. Use quotes for identifiers and text; leave numeric measurements and counts unquoted.

### Using lowercase true, false or none

**Why beginners make it:** Other languages and ordinary writing use different capitalization.

**How to recognize it:** Python reports a `NameError` for `true`, `false` or `none`.

**How to fix it:** Use the exact Python values `True`, `False` and `None`.

### Replacing missing data with zero

**Why beginners make it:** Zero seems easier to calculate with than a missing value.

**How to recognize it:** The notebook can no longer distinguish “measured and equal to zero” from “not measured.” Summary statistics may then be biased.

**How to fix it:** Preserve absence explicitly and document why the value is missing. Do not impute a number until a defensible method has been chosen.

### Giving a variable an unsupported unit

**Why beginners make it:** A decimal value can look familiar enough to guess the unit.

**How to recognize it:** A name such as `elevation_m` makes a claim that cannot be traced to the supplied metadata.

**How to fix it:** Use a neutral name such as `elevation_value` and add a metadata verification note. Rename only after the unit is confirmed.

## Guided Practice

Represent a second published row, `SALS3`, for which no above-ground biomass value is present.

1. Add the Markdown heading `### Guided practice — SALS3`.
2. Create one code cell with these assignments:

   ```python
   plot_id = "SALS3"
   site_name = "Saardu"
   plant_community = "LS"
   species_richness = 5
   biomass_sampled = False
   aboveground_biomass = None
   ```

3. Before running the cell, explain why `aboveground_biomass = 0` would express a different scientific claim.
4. Add print instructions for each variable without copying the earlier print lines.
5. Run the cell and check the output against the assignments.
6. Add a Markdown note: “`None` represents not recorded here; it does not mean zero biomass.”
7. Restart the kernel and run the entire notebook from the first cell. Confirm that Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 still execute in order.

## Independent Challenge

Represent plot `SALS2` without copying the worked example. Use the published values below:

- `SampleID`: `SALS2`;
- `site`: `Saardu`;
- `plantcommunity`: `LS`;
- `Sp_richness`: `6`;
- `CCI_CWM`: `96.5`;
- a biomass value is present.

Choose clear Python variable names and appropriate values. For `CCI_CWM`, use a neutral name such as `cci_cwm_value` until its full definition and measurement convention have been verified. Print every value, then write two sentences explaining why the sample identifier is text and species richness is numeric.

## Scientific Interpretation

The worked example describes one quadrat, not the Saardu site as a whole and not Baltic coastal meadows in general. `species_richness = 7` records a plot-level count. `biomass_sampled = True` records data availability, not ecological magnitude. `elevation_value = 0.530` remains uninterpretable as an elevation measurement until the method and unit are confirmed.

This restraint is part of scientific programming. Code can preserve a number accurately while its scientific meaning remains under-documented. A professional workflow keeps values, metadata and claims aligned.

## Reflection

Write short answers in your private lesson notes:

1. Why should `SALS1` be a string even though its name contains the digit 1?
2. What false claim could be created by replacing a missing biomass value with zero?
3. What information, beyond `0.530`, is needed before interpreting elevation?
4. Which variable name in your notebook best communicates its scientific meaning, and why?

## Submission

Submit all three parts through the lesson task panel:

- **Notebook:** the same `Vegetation_Data_Explorer.ipynb`, now including the SALS1 worked example, SALS3 guided practice, SALS2 challenge and Markdown interpretation.
- **Screenshot:** the SALS2 challenge cell and its output, with the notebook name visible.
- **Written answer:** 120–180 words explaining why data type decisions are scientific decisions. Include one example involving `None` and one involving undocumented units.

A strong submission uses meaningful names, keeps identifiers as text, distinguishes integers from floats, capitalizes Boolean and `None` values correctly, and makes no unsupported claim about units or community codes.

## Portfolio Artifact

**Artifact 02 — Scientific variables notebook**

This checkpoint demonstrates that you can translate one ecological observation into explicit, typed Python values while preserving missingness and metadata uncertainty. It extends Artifact 01 rather than replacing it.

## Further Reading

- [Baltic coastal plant traits 2024 dataset record and citation](https://zenodo.org/records/20083250)
- [Python documentation: an informal introduction](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html)
- [The Turing Way: documenting data](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/rdm/rdm-metadata)

modules.title: Collections: Organizing Ecological Information
modules.description: Choose lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries according to the scientific relationship among species observations, coordinate conventions, trait fields and plot metadata.
modules.lessonContent:
## Learning Outcome

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to choose and create a Python list, tuple, set or dictionary based on the relationship among ecological values. You will be able to explain what ordering, uniqueness, fixed conventions and named fields mean scientifically.

**Prerequisites:** Complete Lessons 1–2 in `Vegetation_Data_Explorer.ipynb`. You should be comfortable running a cell and binding one variable name to one string, number, Boolean or `None` value.

## Why This Matters

One field plot contains related information, not isolated values. A botanist may record an ordered sequence of species observations. A coordinate pair depends on a fixed order. A quality-control step may need the distinct trait fields that are present. A table row connects each field name with one value.

Using the wrong structure can erase that meaning. A set cannot preserve observation order. A list does not label which element is the site or sample identifier. Reversing coordinate order can place a point in the wrong location. A dictionary key that differs by one capital letter can fail to retrieve a value.

Remote sensing scientists spend much of their work organizing relationships: spectral bands and wavelengths, raster dimensions and coordinates, acquisition metadata and values, training samples and class labels. Collections are the first step toward representing those relationships explicitly.

## Scientific Context

The published Baltic coastal plant traits CSV has 25 named fields and 120 rows. We will not load that table until Lesson 7. For now, you will model a tiny portion of the research record around plot `SALS1`.

Two provenance rules matter:

1. The public CSV reports plot-level `Sp_richness` but does not include the species identities used in today’s simplified field-note list. The species list is a teaching record within the Baltic coastal meadow story, not a claim that those identities came from the published table.
2. The public CSV does not provide plot coordinates. We will not fabricate locations. Instead, a tuple will record the coordinate **order convention**—latitude followed by longitude—that future spatial data must follow.

These boundaries demonstrate professional data practice: know which values are sourced, which are instructional and which are unavailable.

## Concept

A **collection** is one Python value that organizes multiple related values. The collection you choose should reflect the scientific relationship.

### List: an ordered, changeable sequence

A list uses square brackets. It preserves item order, allows repeated values and can be extended or changed. A list is suitable for sequential field observations because the position of an observation can matter and the same taxon may be observed more than once.

Python counts positions from zero. The first list item is at position `0`, the second at `1` and so on. This convention will later appear in image bands, table rows and time-series arrays.

### Tuple: a fixed ordered convention

A tuple uses parentheses. Like a list, it preserves order; unlike a list, it cannot be changed in place. A tuple is useful when the positions define a convention that should remain stable, such as `("latitude", "longitude")`.

A tuple does not prevent someone from supplying values in the wrong order. It communicates that the pair is intended to be treated as one fixed structure, so the notebook must still document the convention.

### Set: unique values without a meaningful order

A set uses braces and stores distinct values. Repeated values collapse into one, and display order is not a scientific sequence. A set is useful when the question is “Which distinct trait fields are present?” rather than “In what order were they observed?”

### Dictionary: named fields connected to values

A dictionary uses braces containing `key: value` pairs. Each key is a label used to retrieve its value. A dictionary is a natural model for one table row because `"site"` can be connected to `"Saardu"` and `"Sp_richness"` to `7`.

Dictionary keys are exact. `"site"` and `"Site"` are different strings. Preserving published field names can be important when matching code to metadata.

The four structures are not ranked from simple to advanced. Each answers a different structural question.

## Visual Explanation

![Four-panel diagram comparing a list of species observations, a tuple coordinate convention, a set of unique trait fields and a dictionary of SALS1 metadata.](lesson-media/images/ecological-collections.svg)

Use the captions as a decision guide: ordered observations suggest a list; a fixed convention suggests a tuple; distinct membership suggests a set; named properties suggest a dictionary.

## Worked Example

Add a Markdown heading `## Lesson 3 — Organizing ecological information`. Then type the following code into one new cell, but do not run it yet.

```python
observed_species = [
    "Juncus gerardii",
    "Festuca rubra",
    "Plantago maritima",
]
coordinate_order = ("latitude", "longitude")
trait_fields = {"CCI_CWM", "LA_CWM", "Sp_richness"}
plot_metadata = {
    "SampleID": "SALS1",
    "site": "Saardu",
    "plantcommunity": "LS",
    "Sp_richness": 7,
}

print(observed_species[0])
print(coordinate_order)
print(plot_metadata["site"])
```

The example has seventeen lines, including one blank line. The species names are a simplified instructional field note; the metadata dictionary uses values from the published SALS1 row.

The tuple displays parentheses. The strings inside it display with quotation marks because Python is showing the representation of the complete collection. The first and third print instructions retrieve individual strings, so their output does not show quotes.

## Code Walkthrough

1. `observed_species = [` begins a list and binds it to a descriptive variable name.
2. `"Juncus gerardii",` is the first string at index `0`. The comma separates it from the next item.
3. `"Festuca rubra",` is the second string at index `1`.
4. `"Plantago maritima",` is the third string at index `2`.
5. `]` closes the list. The trailing comma on the previous line is valid and makes later editing cleaner.
6. `coordinate_order = ("latitude", "longitude")` creates a two-item tuple. Position zero is the latitude label and position one is longitude.
7. `trait_fields = {"CCI_CWM", "LA_CWM", "Sp_richness"}` creates a set of three unique published field names. Their display order is not guaranteed to carry meaning.
8. `plot_metadata = {` begins a dictionary for one plot.
9. `"SampleID": "SALS1",` connects the exact field-name key to its string value.
10. `"site": "Saardu",` connects the site key to the site value.
11. `"plantcommunity": "LS",` preserves the published community code without inventing an expansion.
12. `"Sp_richness": 7,` connects the richness field to an integer count.
13. `}` closes the dictionary.
14. The blank line separates data construction from retrieval instructions.
15. `print(observed_species[0])` retrieves the first list item. Index zero means first position.
16. `print(coordinate_order)` displays the complete tuple and therefore makes the fixed order visible.
17. `print(plot_metadata["site"])` looks up the exact key `"site"` and displays its connected value.

## Common Mistakes

### Mixing square brackets, parentheses and braces

**Why beginners make it:** The symbols are visually similar and all can surround multiple items.

**How to recognize it:** Python reports a `SyntaxError`, or the resulting value behaves like a different collection than intended.

**How to fix it:** Link each symbol to a scientific relationship: `[ ]` sequence, `( )` fixed convention, `{ }` unique set or named dictionary pairs.

### Expecting the first list item at index 1

**Why beginners make it:** Everyday counting normally begins at one.

**How to recognize it:** `observed_species[1]` displays `Festuca rubra` rather than the first name. An index beyond the final position produces `IndexError`.

**How to fix it:** Mark positions explicitly while learning: first → 0, second → 1, third → 2.

### Treating set display order as data order

**Why beginners make it:** A printed set appears to have an order on screen.

**How to recognize it:** The order can differ across runs or environments without the membership changing.

**How to fix it:** Use a set only when membership and uniqueness matter. Use a list or tuple when sequence has scientific meaning.

### Creating an empty dictionary when you intended an empty set

**Why beginners make it:** Braces are used by both structures.

**How to recognize it:** `empty = {}` creates a dictionary, not a set.

**How to fix it:** Use `set()` for an empty set. Braces without `key: value` pairs are reserved for an empty dictionary.

### Misspelling a dictionary key

**Why beginners make it:** Human readers treat `site` and `Site` as nearly equivalent.

**How to recognize it:** Python reports `KeyError` even though a similar-looking key is visible.

**How to fix it:** Copy the documented field name exactly and inspect capitalization, underscores and spelling.

### Changing a coordinate convention silently

**Why beginners make it:** Latitude/longitude and x/y conventions differ among tools.

**How to recognize it:** A point appears in an implausible location or outside the study region.

**How to fix it:** Document coordinate order and coordinate reference system next to the data. Never guess or reverse values merely because a map “looks wrong.”

## Scientific Interpretation

The list records a small instructional species sequence; it is not evidence that the public trait table contains species identities. The tuple records a coordinate naming convention; it is not a plot location. The set records which trait field names are of interest; it does not contain their measurements or a meaningful order. The dictionary describes one plot by connecting field names to values; it does not represent the full dataset.

These boundaries are scientifically useful. A data structure can be syntactically valid while communicating the wrong relationship. Selecting a structure is therefore an act of modelling: you decide which properties—order, uniqueness, fixed position or named association—must be preserved.
